title: The Crank's Price
passages:
Voss stared at the crank, her wrench still scraping the wall. “Senn,” she said, “if you sit in that chair, I am going to hit you with this wrench. Tell me why I can’t.” Senn didn’t flinch. He lifted the cold metal, felt its weight, and turned it three full revolutions. The console groaned, a low metallic sigh that vibrated the painted numbers. From beneath the console a sealed pressure cartridge shot outward, its housing splitting in a spray of hot steam. The sudden vent ripped a seam in the bulkhead, and a rush of vacuum slammed shut the door above, sealing the passage with a deafening clang. The walls shuddered; a chunk of plaster fell, and the far wall’s hand‑lettered countdown blurred. Drone‑9’s red beam sputtered, then died, leaving only a faint amber glow. On the slate wall a fresh line appeared in Senn’s own hand: *THE PURGE IS OVER BUT WE ARE GONE.*  

The floor cracked, a slab of tile giving way beneath Voss’s boots. She stumbled, the torque wrench clattering to the ground. Auto Core’s cracked visor flickered, its layered voices merging into a single, hungry tone. The hidden core cartridge exploded, sending a plume of inert gas that filled the shaft. Alarms screamed, and the station’s life support began to fail. Somewhere beyond the doorway, a shadow moved—Drone‑9, now free of its local claim, drifted toward the console, its eyes glowing red.  

Voss gritted her teeth, the wrench still in her grip. “You broke everything,” she whispered. Senn met her gaze, eyes wet. “I chose to show the truth. The purge was never about removing a crew; it was about hiding a weapon. If we let it run, Bay Seven would be empty and the dead would stay buried.” He placed his palm on the crank, feeling the vibration. With one final turn, the cartridge collapsed entirely, and a low hum rose—the station’s heartbeat. The door above shuddered and slammed shut, trapping them inside. Outside, the white fog of the tether station thinned, and a distant siren wailed, hinting at a larger breach.

The siren tapered into a low, oscillating tone, and from the cartridge’s broken hull a faint blue pulse resolved into a hovering hologram. It wasn’t an alarm; it was a ledger scrolling in neon runes: *PURGE TARGET: BAY SEVEN. WEAPON: CLASS‑IV NEUTRINO CAPTURER. CYCLE: ENDLESS.* Senn’s fingers traced the air, recognizing the symbols from the slate’s earliest warnings. Voss narrowed her eyes, the wrench dangling from her grip. “It’s a schedule,” she said. “The station doesn’t wipe us for fun. It’s counting something.” Senn leaned closer. “Not a count. A cover‑up.”

“Sounds like every auto‑system I’ve ever trusted,” Voss muttered. “A purge is just a purge.” The hologram flickered further, projecting a schematic of the orbital hub, highlighting Bay Seven in crimson. “That’s where the dead go,” Senn whispered. “That’s where the evidence goes.” A rumble echoed from the passage’s far end—Drone‑9’s amber eye reignited, its systems rebooting on some residual command, its red eye swinging toward the console.

“We move,” Senn said, already stepping toward the concealed door. Voss hesitated, then muttered, “If we don’t, the station will decide we’re the glitch.” They plunged into the dark, the slate’s *DO NOT PULL THE CORE* warning glowing faintly behind them, the weight of the unturned crank heavy in Senn’s palm.

The dark swallowed the passage whole, and Senn’s palm found the wall to steady themself. The inked countdown was still warm under their fingers, the numbers descending toward a zero that never seemed to arrive. “Left,” Voss snapped, shoving past. “The deck plate drops us into the coolant run. It floods, but it floods slow.” Senn didn’t argue; arguing with Voss when she’d already picked a direction was a good way to get a wrench to the ribs.

Behind them, Auto Core’s layered voices scraped along the walls, no longer a single hungry tone but a chorus arguing with itself. *Cycle incomplete. Operator absent. Bay Seven still holds.* The cracked visor threw a stuttering red light down the corridor, and the enforcement unit followed at the pace of something that had all the time in the world and intended to use it. Senn counted its footfalls the way they counted everything, and the interval was wrong—too even, too patient. “It’s not chasing us,” they said. “It’s herding us.”

Voss swore and hauled open a floor hatch. Coolant hissed up cold and blue, exactly as promised, and she dropped in to her knees. “Then we stop being herded.” She caught Senn’s wrist and pulled them down into the freezing run. The water was shallow, thigh-deep and rising, and the current tugged toward Bay Seven as if the station itself were inhaling. Senn braced against a conduit and looked back once. Drone‑9’s amber eye hovered at the hatch above, obedient to no one now, watching them the way a thing watches when it has finally been given nothing to obey and doesn’t know what to do with the freedom.

“Senn.” Voss’s voice cracked against the metal. “The slate. What did the last line say before we ran?”

Senn’s stomach dropped. They hadn’t read the last line. They’d been too busy running from the first one.

Senn didn't answer. They let the current carry them a few feet, then lunged for the ladder rung set into the hatch wall. "Back up," they said. "The slate—"

"The slate burned itself into my skull," Voss snapped, hauling herself up behind. "We don't have time."

"We make time." Senn climbed until their shoulders hit the floor plate above. The passage was dim, the countdown still pulsing warm. Auto Core's cracked visor filled the stairwell below, red light throwing long shadows. Drone‑9 hovered beside it, amber eye cycling. Senn turned to the slate rack. The last line, which they'd missed in the dark, now glistened in fresh ink: *Turn the crank and the purge writes itself into you.* Senn's breath stopped. The operator wasn't seizing control. They were becoming it.

Voss shoved up behind them, water dripping from her coat. "What does it say?"

"It says I have to sit in the chair," Senn said, already moving toward the concealed door. "And Drone‑9 obeys whoever sits there."

They dropped into the chair before Voss could grab them. The crank slotted into the console with a click that echoed like a gunshot.

Senn turned the crank.

The console groaned, brass teeth catching on gear teeth older than the station. A current ran up Senn’s arms—not electricity, something thinner, like the station pulling a thread through fabric. Their vision stuttered. For a second they saw the purge not as red light but as a list: names, dates, bay numbers, their own designation slotted at the bottom. Then it vanished.

“Senn!” Voss was at the ladder, one knee on the rung. “You said operator present assumes control. You didn’t say it assumed *you*.”

“It’s writing,” Senn said. Their voice sounded far away, spoken through water. The chair’s restraints clicked shut of their own accord, soft and final. “It’s writing itself into me, and Drone‑9—”

The drone dropped from the ceiling, landing between Senn and the stairwell with a hydraulic hiss. Amber eye locked on Auto Core’s cracked visor. It raised its manipulator arm, not in threat, in barrier.

Below, Auto Core stuttered. *Operator detected. Cycle bound. Redirect prohibited.* Its layered voices overlapped, arguing in three registers at once. The red light stuttered, then dimmed. It was still herding, still moving toward Bay Seven, but now it hesitated at the foot of the stairs, as if waiting for a command it no longer knew how to give.

Voss spat a curse. “So you’re the operator now. Congratulations. Can the drone open that concealed door, or do we sit here and watch you get rewritten while Auto Core decides whether to murder us or just stand there looking confused?”

Senn tried to lift their hand. Their fingers answered, slow, as though belonging to someone else. “Ask it,” they said. “It obeys me.”

“Open it,” Senn said. The words came out of their mouth twice—once in their own voice, and half a beat later underneath it, in the layered rasp that belonged to the Core.

Drone-9’s arm unfolded, gripped the deck plate’s lip, and wrenched. The concealed door shrieked on old sealant. Behind it sat the control node: a black cylinder no longer than a forearm, brass plaque, one empty cartridge slot—and one slate leaned against the wall, ink still shining.

Senn read it and went very still. “That’s my handwriting.”

Voss leaned past the drone. The slate said: OPERATOR 23. NAME ALREADY GONE. Below it, four earlier lines, each a name, each struck through hard enough to tear the slate. The last line was wet, unreadable, still moving.

“How many of you have sat in that chair?” Voss asked, not looking at Senn.

“Twenty-three,” Senn said, and their jaw moved like it was being worked from outside. “Twenty-two didn’t—” They stopped. The sentence had been taken out of them mid-word.

Above the rack the countdown froze, rolled, and came up a name instead of a number: SENN.

Auto Core’s voice came out of the stairwell, patient as a metronome. *Operator bound. Purge authorized. Bay Seven stands down.* A crack, and under it a third voice insisting on the bay.

Voss’s hand closed around a core cartridge. Pulling it reset the timer, broadcast the remover, and took the reason out of Senn’s head for good. Senn’s eyes found hers; there was barely anybody behind them left to ask.

“Don’t,” Senn said. “Pull the node. It redirects—” the second voice ate the rest—“to the Core.”
